title: What is an index in SQL, what are the types (primary, unique, non-unique, composite, clustered vs non-clustered), and how do you create one with `CREATE INDEX`?
shortTitle: What is an index in SQL, the types (primary, unique, non-unique, composite, clustered vs non-clustered), and how to create one with `CREATE INDEX`

s1_definition.profdef: A database index is an auxiliary on-disk data structure, usually a balanced B-tree, that stores a sorted copy of one or more column values together with pointers to the full rows. It lets the database locate matching rows in logarithmic time instead of scanning every row, at the cost of extra storage and slower writes because the index must be maintained on every insert, update, and delete. Index types include the primary-key index (unique, not-null, one per table, usually clustered), unique indexes, non-unique indexes, composite (multi-column) indexes, and the physical distinction between clustered (the table rows are physically ordered by the key) and non-clustered (a separate structure that points back to the rows).
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India customer ledger as a giant book with ten million accounts. Without an index, finding Rajesh's account SAV2001 means reading every page from the first until you hit it — a full table scan. An index is like the alphabetical thumb-tabs and the index at the back of the book: it is a small sorted list of account numbers with the exact page where each one lives. Now finding SAV2001 takes a few jumps instead of reading the whole book. A clustered index means the book itself is physically sorted by account number; a non-clustered index is a separate little index card box that says "SAV2001 is on page 4,502."
s1_definition.oneliner: An index is a sorted shortcut that trades a little write cost and disk space for massively faster reads.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A database index is an auxiliary on-disk data structure, usually a balanced B-tree, that stores a sorted copy of one or more column values together with pointers to the full rows. It lets the database locate matching rows in logarithmic time instead of scanning every row, at the cost of extra storage and slower writes because the index must be maintained on every insert, update, and delete. Index types include the primary-key index (unique, not-null, one per table, usually clustered), unique indexes, non-unique indexes, composite (multi-column) indexes, and the physical distinction between clustered (the table rows are physically ordered by the key) and non-clustered (a separate structure that points back to the rows).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the National Bank of India customer ledger as a giant book with ten million accounts. Without an index, finding Rajesh's account SAV2001 means reading every page from the first until you hit it — a full table scan. An index is like the alphabetical thumb-tabs and the index at the back of the book: it is a small sorted list of account numbers with the exact page where each one lives. Now finding SAV2001 takes a few jumps instead of reading the whole book. A clustered index means the book itself is physically sorted by account number; a non-clustered index is a separate little index card box that says "SAV2001 is on page 4,502."

**One line to remember:** An index is a sorted shortcut that trades a little write cost and disk space for massively faster reads.

sections.s2_technical:
A primary-key index is created automatically when you declare a `PRIMARY KEY`. It enforces two rules — every value is unique and no value is null — and in most engines it becomes the clustered index, meaning the actual table rows are stored in primary-key order. For example `CREATE TABLE accounts (id VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY, ...)` gives you a clustered B-tree on `id` for free.

A unique index enforces uniqueness on a column that is not the primary key. At the bank every account has a government PAN number that must be unique but is not the primary key, so you write `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ux_accounts_pan ON accounts(pan)`. Any insert that duplicates a PAN fails with a constraint violation.

A non-unique index allows duplicate values and exists purely for lookup speed. Many accounts share the same branch code, so `CREATE INDEX ix_accounts_branch ON accounts(branch_code)` speeds up "all accounts in branch MUM001" without forbidding duplicates.

A composite index covers more than one column in a defined order, such as `CREATE INDEX ix_txn_acct_date ON transactions(account_id, created_at)`. The column order matters enormously because the index is sorted first by `account_id` and then by `created_at` within each account.

The clustered versus non-clustered distinction is physical. A clustered index determines the actual row storage order, so there can be only one per table. A non-clustered index is a separate B-tree whose leaf nodes hold the indexed columns plus a pointer (the primary key or a physical row locator) back to the full row, so you can have many of them. In PostgreSQL the primary key is technically a non-clustered unique index over a heap, while SQL Server and MySQL/InnoDB make the primary key the clustered index — a nuance worth stating in an interview.

You create an index with `CREATE INDEX index_name ON table_name(column_list)`, optionally `UNIQUE`, and you drop it with `DROP INDEX`. A senior nuance: every extra index slows down writes and consumes space, so you index for the queries you actually run, confirmed by the execution plan, not speculatively.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India transactions table has grown to two hundred million rows. The mobile app screen "show me my last ten transactions" runs `WHERE account_id = 'SAV2001' ORDER BY created_at DESC` and it takes four seconds because the database reads every row. This is exactly what a composite index fixes: an index on `(account_id, created_at)` lets the database jump straight to Rajesh's rows already sorted by date.

Problem 2 — The compliance team keeps accidentally creating two accounts with the same PAN. This is exactly what a unique index does: it refuses the duplicate at the database level so a bug in the application cannot corrupt the data.

Problem 3 — The operations team wants to see "all accounts in the Mumbai branch" and duplicates are expected. This is exactly what a non-unique index does: fast lookup, duplicates allowed.

The mini-project is a Spring Boot settlement service. We define an `Account` entity and a `Transaction` entity, a Flyway migration that creates the tables and all four index types, a repository with derived queries that rely on those indexes, and a service method that fetches Rajesh's recent transactions. We will log the query and show how the index turns a full scan into a fast seek.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build the service
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run it against PostgreSQL
java -jar target/account-index-service-1.0.0.jar --spring.profiles.active=dev

# Confirm the database is actually using the index (do NOT assume)
psql -d bankdb -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE account_id = 'SAV2001' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10;"
# Expect: Index Scan using ix_txn_acct_date  (not Seq Scan)
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the mobile app requests the last ten transactions for account SAV2001.

Step 1 — The request arrives at `TransactionService.recentTransactions("SAV2001", 10)`. The data is still just an account id and a limit held in memory.

Step 2 — The repository translates the derived method name into SQL: `SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE account_id = 'SAV2001' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10`.

Step 3 — The query planner sees the predicate on `account_id` and the sort on `created_at`. It recognizes that the composite index `ix_txn_acct_date` is sorted exactly this way, so it chooses an index scan instead of a sequential scan.

Step 4 — The database walks the B-tree to the first entry for `SAV2001`, then reads backward along the already-sorted `created_at` values, stopping after ten entries. It never touches the other 199,999,990 rows.

Step 5 — Ten row pointers lead to ten full rows, which are returned to the service, mapped to entities, and handed back to the controller as a JSON list.

```text
2026-10-25 13:40:01 INFO  TransactionService - Fetching last 10 transactions for account SAV2001
2026-10-25 13:40:01 INFO  TransactionService - Returned 10 transactions using index ix_txn_acct_date
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Client: GET /api/v1/accounts/SAV2001/transactions?limit=10
    │
    ▼
  TransactionController
    │ path var accountId=SAV2001, query limit=10
    ▼
  TransactionService.recentTransactions("SAV2001", 10)
    │
    ▼
  TransactionRepository (Spring Data JPA)
    │ SQL: WHERE account_id='SAV2001' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10
    ▼
  Query Planner
    │ chooses: Index Scan using ix_txn_acct_date (NOT Seq Scan)
    ▼
  B-tree ix_txn_acct_date
    │ seek to (SAV2001, *) → read 10 entries backward by created_at
    ▼
  Heap: fetch 10 full rows
    │
    ▼
  Response: 200 OK  [10 TransactionResponse JSON objects]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
An index is an auxiliary sorted data structure, almost always a B-tree, that lets the database find rows in logarithmic time instead of scanning the entire table. The trade-off is that every index costs extra disk space and slows down inserts, updates, and deletes because the index must be maintained, so you create indexes deliberately for the queries you actually run.

The main types are the primary-key index, which enforces uniqueness and not-null and is usually the clustered index that physically orders the rows; the unique index, which enforces uniqueness on a non-primary-key column; the non-unique index, which is purely for lookup speed and allows duplicates; and the composite index, which spans multiple columns in a specific order. The clustered versus non-clustered distinction is physical: a clustered index is the table itself sorted by the key, so there is only one, while non-clustered indexes are separate structures that point back to the rows, so you can have many.

At the National Bank of India our transactions table had grown past two hundred million rows and the "last ten transactions" screen took four seconds because the database scanned every row. I added a composite index on account id and created-at in that order, so the planner could seek straight to the customer's rows already sorted by date and stop after ten. The screen dropped to a few milliseconds. I also added a unique index on the PAN column so a bug in the application could never create two accounts with the same tax number, and a plain non-unique index on branch code for operations lookups.

The senior habit I always mention is that I never assume an index is being used. I create it with `CREATE INDEX`, then I run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` and confirm the plan says Index Scan rather than Sequential Scan, because indexing the wrong column order or wrapping a column in a function silently defeats the index.
